chapters.title: The Puck That Would Not Behave
paragraphs: Thwack!
Lincoln's stick hit the puck. But the puck did not zoom into the net. It hopped. It flipped. Then it rolled away on its edge like a runaway cookie and hid under his BMX bike.
“Not again,” said Lincoln.

He was in the garage, where he practised his shot almost every day after school. A hockey net stood against the back wall. Above it hung a poster of Sidney Crosby, the captain of the Pittsburgh Penguins, in his black and gold jersey. Number 87.

Lincoln wore number 87 too. He knew a lot about Sidney Crosby. He knew that Sid was born on the seventh day of the eighth month, in 1987, and that is why he picked 87. He also knew that when Sid was a kid, he shot pucks in his basement for hours and hours. He missed the net so many times that the family's clothes dryer ended up covered in dents.
“If Sid can dent a dryer, I can hit a net,” Lincoln said. He fished the puck out from under the bike and tried again.
Thwack! Hop. Flip. Roll.
The door to the house opened. His sister Ivy came out, and his brother Jaxson was right behind her.
“We heard a lot of thwacking,” said Ivy.
“And not much scoring,” said Jaxson. He grinned.

Lincoln did not grin back. He was thinking. “Here is the strange part,” he said. “At the rink on Saturday, the puck stayed flat and slid smoothly. Here, the very same kind of puck bounces around like popcorn. Why?”
“Because the garage floor isn't ice?” said Ivy.
“Maybe,” said Lincoln. “But that only explains the sliding. It doesn't explain the bouncing.”
Jaxson picked up the puck and squeezed it. “It's just a puck.”
“Nothing is just anything,” said Lincoln. That was his favourite thing to say.
He ran inside and came back with a blue notebook. On the cover, in thick black marker, it said: LINCOLN'S QUESTION NOTEBOOK. KEEP OUT (unless you have an answer).
The notebook was full of questions. Why is the sky blue? How do planes stay up? Why can't you tickle yourself? Some of the questions had answers written under them. Lots of them did not. Not yet.
Lincoln turned to a clean page and wrote carefully:
Question 112: Why does a puck bounce at home but not at the rink?
Then he looked up at the poster. On Saturday his team, the Fireants, had a big game against the Thunder. The Thunder had not lost all season.
“Five days,” said Lincoln. “I have five days to solve this mystery.”

chapters.title: A Clue at Recess
paragraphs: The next morning it was so cold that Lincoln could see his breath. At recess he ran straight to the gaga ball pit with his friends Owen and Maya.

Gaga ball was the best game at school. The pit had eight short wooden walls. You slapped the ball with your hand and tried to hit other players below the knee. If the ball hit you, you were out. The last player in the pit was the winner.
“Ga! Ga! Ball!” everyone shouted, and the game began.
Lincoln jumped. He dodged. He slapped the ball hard at Owen. But the ball did not bounce far. It hit the ground with a dull thud and rolled slowly, like it was sleepy.
“This ball is flat,” said Maya. She gave it a poke.
“It feels like a rock,” said Owen. “My soccer ball does that in winter too. It's like kicking a brick.”

After lunch the sun came out. The ball had been sitting on the warm window shelf in the classroom all morning. This time, when the game began, the ball went wild. It sprang off the walls. It bounced right over the top of the pit, and a kindergarten kid had to chase it.
Lincoln stopped in the middle of the game. He stood very still.
“Same ball,” he said slowly. “Cold this morning. Warm now. Sleepy this morning. Bouncy now.”
Bop! The ball hit his shoe.
“You're out, Lincoln!” yelled Maya.
Lincoln didn't even mind. He climbed out of the pit, smiling. He had a clue.
When the game ended, he told Owen and Maya all about the puck that would not behave.
“Maybe cold things are just less bouncy,” said Owen.
“That's a hypothesis!” said Lincoln.
“A hippo what?” said Owen.
“A hypothesis. It's a smart guess that you can test. Scientists make them all the time.”
Their teacher, Ms. Park, was walking by with her coffee. “That's right,” she said. “But remember, a guess is only a guess until you test it.”
“Then let's test it,” said Maya. “I can bring a tape measure.”
“I can bring two more pucks,” said Owen.
“My garage. Tomorrow after school,” said Lincoln. “And tonight, I am going to put one puck in the freezer.”

chapters.title: The Freezer Test
paragraphs: On Wednesday after school, the garage turned into a science lab.

Three pucks sat in a row on the workbench. Puck one had spent the whole night in the freezer, between the peas and the ice cream. It was so cold that it had frost on it. Puck two had sat on a shelf, so it was the same temperature as the room. Puck three had soaked in a bowl of warm water.
“First we need a way to measure the bounce,” said Lincoln.
That was a job for Lego. Lincoln and Jaxson built a tall, thin tower. They changed the colour every ten bricks. Red, then blue, then yellow, then green, then white, then black. Sixty bricks high.
“Now we can see how high each puck bounces,” said Lincoln. “But it has to be a fair test. That means we change only one thing. The temperature. Everything else must stay the same.”

So they made rules. Every puck would be dropped from the very top of the tower. Every puck would land flat on the same spot on the floor. Jaxson would do all the dropping. Ivy would film each drop in slow motion, so they could see the top of every bounce. Maya would write down the results.
“Predictions first,” said Lincoln. A prediction is what you think will happen before you try it.
“I say the warm one bounces highest,” said Owen.
“I say they all bounce the same,” said Jaxson. “A puck is a puck.”
Jaxson dropped the warm puck first. Bonk! It jumped up past the red bricks, past the blue bricks, and into the yellow.
Next came the room puck. Bonk! It reached the blue bricks.
Last came the frozen puck. Thunk. It barely hopped at all. It did not even get out of the red.
They tested each puck three times, just to be sure. Every time, the answer was the same.
“The frozen one is lazy,” said Jaxson.
“Not lazy,” said Lincoln. “Stiff.” He pulled a big book called How the World Works off the shelf and found the page about rubber.

“A puck is made of rubber,” he read. “Rubber is made of long, tangled chains, a bit like a bowl of tiny noodles. When rubber is warm, the chains can wiggle and stretch, so they spring back. That makes a bounce. When rubber is cold, the chains get stiff. They can't spring back as well.”
“So a cold puck stays down,” said Maya.
“Our hypothesis was right!” said Owen.
Lincoln opened his notebook to Question 112. But he did not write ANSWERED. Not yet.
“We know cold pucks don't bounce,” he said. “But are the pucks at the rink really frozen? And why do they slide so far? We only have half an answer.”
“Who would know the other half?” asked Ivy.
Lincoln smiled. “Tomorrow is hockey practice. I know just who to ask.”

chapters.title: The Secret in the Cooler
paragraphs: On Thursday, Lincoln got to the arena early. Coach Bell was by the bench, filling water bottles.
“Coach,” said Lincoln, “are the pucks at the rink frozen?”
Coach Bell laughed. “Who told you my secret?” She flipped open a small blue cooler. Inside, on a bed of ice, sat a stack of pucks.
“I knew it!” said Lincoln.
“A warm puck bounces and rolls,” said Coach Bell. “A cold puck stays flat. In the NHL, they keep the game pucks in a freezer. They even swap in fresh cold ones during the game.”
Just then a deep rumble filled the arena. A big machine rolled out onto the ice. Most people call it a Zamboni. It drove in slow, neat loops, and behind it the ice turned dark and shiny.
The driver was a woman named Dot, with a long grey braid. When she finished, Lincoln was waiting by the gate with his notebook.
“Excuse me,” he said. “What does your machine do? And why is ice so slippery?”
Dot's eyes twinkled. “Finally, somebody asks! First, a sharp blade shaves off the rough top of the ice. Next, the machine scoops up all that snow. Last, it spreads a thin layer of hot water.”
“Hot water? On ice?” said Lincoln.
“Hot water,” said Dot. “It melts into every scratch and crack. Then it freezes as flat as glass.”
“And the slippery part?”
“Ah. Have you heard of friction?” asked Dot. Lincoln shook his head.

“Friction is the rubbing that slows things down when they slide. Rub your hands together, fast.” Lincoln did. His hands got warm. “That's friction. A garage floor has lots of it. Carpet has even more. But ice has hardly any. The very top of the ice is a layer so thin that you can't see it, and it acts a bit like water. Your skates and your puck glide along on top of it.”
Lincoln wrote as fast as he could. Friction. Less friction means more sliding.

At practice that day, his shots stayed flat. They skimmed across the ice and smacked into the net. But near the end, the ice was cut up and covered in snow from all the skating. His last pass to Owen slowed down and stopped short.
“See that?” called Coach Bell. “Snowy ice is slow ice. Remember that on Saturday.”
Lincoln nodded. He wrote that down too.

chapters.title: Friction at the Bike Park
paragraphs: On Friday after school, Lincoln, Owen and Maya took their BMX bikes to the bike park.

Lincoln pulled on his helmet, his gloves and his elbow pads. Then he rolled to the top of the start hill and looked down at the track. It was a long loop of packed dirt, with bumps called rollers and tall, curved corners called berms.
“Race you!” shouted Owen.
Down they went. Lincoln did not even need to pedal. He pushed down on the back of each roller and got lighter over the top, and his bike went faster and faster. Riders call that pumping.

As he rode, he thought about friction. He could not stop thinking about it now. His tires were gripping the dirt. That was friction. When he squeezed his brakes, the pads rubbed on the wheel and slowed him down. That was friction too.
“So friction isn't always bad,” he said to himself. “On a bike, you need it!”
He was thinking so hard that he came into the big berm much too fast. And he did not see the patch of loose gravel.
His front tire hit the gravel. The little stones rolled under it like marbles. The tire lost its grip. The bike slid one way and Lincoln slid the other.
Whump! He landed in the dirt.
Maya skidded to a stop beside him. “Are you okay?”
Lincoln sat up. There was dirt on his chin and a long scrape on his elbow pad. He wiggled his arms and legs. Everything worked.
“I'm okay,” he said. “I just found a spot with no friction.”
Maya laughed so hard that she nearly fell off her own bike.

Lincoln picked up his bike and looked back at the gravel. “On the ice, I want less friction, so the puck can glide,” he said. “On my bike, I want more friction, so my tires can grip. And when I stop on skates, I dig my blades in sideways. I make friction on purpose!”
“So is friction good or bad?” asked Owen.
“Neither,” said Lincoln. “You just have to know when you need it.”
He rode the big berm again. This time he went a little slower and stayed on the hard, packed dirt. His tires held. He zipped around the corner and let out a whoop.
That night he added a line to his notebook. Friction: sometimes a friend, sometimes a pest. The trick is knowing which.

chapters.title: The Lego Launcher
paragraphs: On Friday night, Lincoln could not sit still. The big game was tomorrow, and his tummy felt like it was full of jumping frogs.

To calm down, he played Roblox with Owen and Maya. They picked an obby, which is an obstacle course full of jumps and traps. Level nine had a floor made of ice. Lincoln's character ran onto it and could not stop. He slid right off the edge.
“Whoever built this level knows about friction,” said Lincoln.
Then he had an idea. He said goodbye to his friends and went to find Ivy and Jaxson.
“I need to see how a puck slides on different floors,” he said. “But I can't just push it with my hand. I might push harder one time and softer the next. That would not be a fair test.”
“So build a machine,” said Ivy.

They tipped the big bin of Lego onto the floor. Lincoln built a ramp with smooth tiles on top. Jaxson built two strong towers to hold it up. Ivy added a little gate at the top. When you lifted the gate, the puck slid down the ramp. It started the same way every single time.
“The Lego Launcher is ready,” said Jaxson in a deep robot voice.
First they tried the carpet in the living room. The puck slid down the ramp, hit the carpet and stopped almost at once. Ivy measured. “Nine centimetres.”
Next they tried the wooden floor in the hall. The puck slid much farther. “Seventy centimetres!”
“Now we need ice,” said Lincoln.
Ivy had already thought of that. Earlier, she had poured a little water onto a metal baking tray and put it in the freezer. Now she carried it out. It was a tiny, perfect rink.

They set the tray at the bottom of the ramp. Jaxson lifted the gate. The puck zipped down the ramp, shot across the ice, flew off the end of the tray, skidded over the kitchen floor and vanished under the fridge.
Nobody said anything for a second. Then all three of them burst out laughing. Jaxson got it back with a hockey stick.
“One more test,” said Lincoln. He scraped some frost out of the freezer and sprinkled it over the tray like snow. This time the puck wobbled, slowed down and stopped before the end.
“Just like Coach Bell said,” whispered Lincoln. “Snowy ice is slow ice.”
He climbed into bed and looked at the Sidney Crosby poster he kept on his wall there too. The frogs in his tummy had gone quiet.
“When the ice gets snowy tomorrow,” he said, “I'll know what to do.”

chapters.title: The Big Game
paragraphs: The arena was loud on Saturday. Ivy and Jaxson had seats right behind the glass. Ivy held up a sign that said GO 87!
The Thunder were fast. They scored first. Then they scored again. Maya blasted a shot from far out to make it 2–1, but that was all the Fireants could do.

With five minutes left in the game, the Fireants were still behind. The ice was cut up and covered in snow. Owen tried a pass to Lincoln. It slowed down and stopped short. A Thunder player scooped it up and skated away.
Back on the bench, Owen thumped his stick on the boards. “My passes keep dying!”

“It's not you,” said Lincoln. “It's the ice. It's snowy, so there's more friction now. The puck slows down faster. We have to pass harder. And if the puck is bouncing, we stop it flat before we shoot.”
Coach Bell had been listening. “You heard the scientist,” she said. “Hard passes. Flat pucks. Go!”

They jumped over the boards. Maya got the puck behind her own net and fired a hard pass up the ice. It bounced toward Lincoln on its edge. His heart was pounding. He wanted to shoot right away. But he waited one tiny second and pressed the puck flat with his stick.
Then he saw Owen, all alone in front of the net. Lincoln snapped a pass, hard and flat. Owen tipped it in.
It was 2–2! The crowd roared.
One minute left. The Thunder had the puck in their own end. A Thunder player tried a long, soft pass across the snowy ice.
Lincoln knew what was going to happen before it happened. The pass slowed down. It was never going to get there. He raced in and stole it.
Now there was nobody between Lincoln and the goalie.
The puck was wobbling. He tapped it flat. He thought about the dents in Sidney Crosby's dryer. He thought about a thousand shots in the garage. Then he shot low, along the ice.
The puck slid under the goalie's pad and into the net.
The horn blared. Fireants 3, Thunder 2!
The whole team piled on top of Lincoln. Behind the glass, Ivy and Jaxson jumped up and down and banged on the boards.
Afterwards, Coach Bell tapped him on the helmet. “Slow ice. Hard passes. Flat pucks. Where did you learn all that?”
Lincoln grinned. “From a freezer, a Zamboni driver, a bike crash and a baking tray.”

chapters.title: Question 113
paragraphs: On Monday, Ms. Park let Lincoln share his discovery with the whole class.
He stood at the front with Coach Bell's blue cooler. He took out a frozen puck. Then he took a warm puck from his pocket. He held them both up high.
“Predictions, please,” he said. “Which one will bounce higher?”
Half the class pointed at the cold puck. Half pointed at the warm one. Lincoln let go.
Bonk! went the warm puck, and it hopped up to his knee. Thunk went the frozen puck. It hardly moved.
“Whoa,” said the whole class.

Lincoln told them the three things he had learned. Warm rubber bounces and cold rubber does not. Friction is the rubbing that slows sliding things down. And ice is slippery because it has hardly any friction at all.
“And how did you find all this out?” asked Ms. Park.
“I asked a question,” said Lincoln. “Then I made a guess. Then I tested it.”
At afternoon recess, the sun was warm and the gaga ball was as bouncy as a rabbit. Lincoln kept his hits low and fast. For the first time all year, he was the last player left in the pit.
When he got home, Ivy and Jaxson were waiting for him at the kitchen table. Each of them had a brand new notebook.
“Question one,” Ivy read out. “Why does hot water make the ice smoother than cold water?”
“Question one,” Jaxson read out. “How does a freezer make things cold, anyway?”
Lincoln laughed. “Those are good ones. I don't know the answers.”
“Yet,” said Ivy.
Up in his room, Lincoln opened his own notebook to Question 112. Under it he wrote, in big letters: ANSWERED. He drew a small puck beside it, with a happy face.

Then he saw his baseball glove sitting on the shelf. The snow would melt soon, and baseball season would begin. Last summer he had watched a pitcher throw a ball that curved in the air, like magic. He had wondered about it ever since.
But it wasn't magic. Nothing is just anything.
Lincoln turned to a clean page, and he wrote:
Question 113: How does a baseball curve?
